utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I was informed that there was one preliminary matter to be raised. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, good morning Mr. President. Yes, this is in response to your question yesterday regarding the Defence document D00019. It was a 9 July document regarding the BiH Srebrenica municipality Presidency. We looked into where that came from, and it came from a search by SFOR in 1999 of the 3rd Corps of the Bosnian Serb army, which was the -- formerly the Drina Corps and a search of the 503rd Brigade which was formerly the Zvornik Brigade. A number the documents were seized by SFOR, scanned, and then we got CDs and then the originals were given back. Those collections have been provided to the Defence for years now. We've all found them useful and reliable, various documents, so we infer that they may have been retrieved by the VRS when the VRS overran Srebrenica because there are quite a few Muslim documents in that collection. But that's just an inference. In any event, that -- it's -- we have no problem with this -- this collection or its authentication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that information, Mr. McCloskey. While waiting for the witness to be brought in -- and if the Prosecution is ready, we can ask the witness to be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Prosecution is ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have a brief matter which I can address when the witness is arriving. It is about P143. The Chamber notes the Prosecution's request to the Registry, which was sent per e-mail on the 15th of April, in follow-up of a discussions in court at transcript pages 9517 and 9518, to replace the existing surrogate sheet for P143, which is MFI'd, with a revised surrogate sheet bearing doc ID number 22477A-REV. The Chamber instructs the Registry to make this replacement and hereby admits P143 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Boering, I take it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Boering, before you give evidence -- apparently Mr. Boering is not receiving ... on what channel is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yup, prima.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You now hear me in a language you understand. Yes. Mr. Boering, before you give evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is handed out to you but let's wait for one second. That's an English text. If you feel comfortable to make the solemn declaration in English, it's fine. Otherwise you can do it in your own language. Which one would you prefer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] English is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, then please may I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Boering. Please be seated. Mr. Boering, as you may have noticed, I addressed you as Mr. Boering. I also noted that in a previous case you were addressed by your rank and your name. It's not in any way in depreciation of your rank, but we have the habit in this courtroom to address all our witnesses as Mr. Or Mrs., just for you to know. Mr. Boering, you will first be examined by Mr. Shin. Mr. Shin is counsel for the Prosecution and you find him to your right. Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And let me just say good morning, Your Honours, and good morning to counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Boering. Could you please state for the record your full name.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: My full name is Pieter Boering.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Is it correct that you provided signed statements to the Office of the Prosecutor at this Tribunal in September of 1995 and February of 1998?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And have you previously testified before this Tribunal in five cases: Namely, Krstic, in March of 2000; Blagojevic in June of 2003; Popovic, in September of 2006; Tolimir in December 2010; and Karadzic in November 2011?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: In preparation for your testimony in the Tolimir and Karadzic cases, did you review your testimony in the Popovic case?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, I did, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And in preparing to give evidence here today, did you also have a chance to review your testimony in the Popovic case?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, I did that last week.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could I please have 65 ter 28791 brought up on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And, just briefly, Mr. Boering, it -- do you recognise at least not -- the top part of this page to be from your Popovic testimony, which you reviewed for your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes. It looks like a familiar piece of paper, although it's a very short fragment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Perhaps we could just turn to the next page as well to confirm that this is the transcript that -- this is from the transcript that you had reviewed.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, this is familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Boering.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution would propose to tender the 92 ter transcripts at the end of the direct examination of the witness. There are some matters which may be clarifications which we would prefer to take through in chronological order in the direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You want to tender it at the end? I already, at this moment, I express some concern about -- about more or less ignoring on a more frequent basis the clear preference of the Chamber to receive 92 ter evidence through statements rather than through transcripts. The Chamber will further consider whether we can continue like this. I already announce this at this very moment, but since there are only two of the Judges present at this moment, I'd rather keep that for a later moment. And I have one additional question for Mr. Boering in respect of his confirmation that this is what he reviewed. Mr. Boering, you have been provided with an English version of your testimony, whereas you gave your testimony in the Dutch language which was then translated. Are you -- is your familiarity with the English language sufficient for you to confirm that this is your testimony; and did you notice anything in the English language which -- which you -- puzzled you as far as your own testimony is concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I have to say that I prefer to give testimony in my own language before the Court, that this is more convenient for my own memory and for my own experience. But, in general, my command of the English language is sufficient, and therefore I have no problems reading documents on the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we'll -- you'll wait -- perhaps we already assign a number to it --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- in order for it to be MFI'd. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28791 receives number P1139, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1139 is marked for identification. You may proceed, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And with your permission, may I now read a summary of the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so. You have explained to Mr. Boering what the purpose of it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I don't recall if I specifically indicated, but he is -- I did explain that there would be a procedure similar to that followed in the Tolimir and Karadzic cases in which that did occur.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Boering, the whole purpose of reading a summary is that the public is aware of the content of your previous testimony which enables them to better understand any questions that will be put to you after that. Please proceed, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I will now proceed with the summary of the witness's evidence. Colonel Pieter Boering arrived in Srebrenica on 3rd of January 1995 as a major in DutchBat where he served as a liaison officer with the ABiH and the VRS, as well as the civilian leadership on both sides and with NGOs. The witness describes the humanitarian situation in the enclave and the deteriorating situation in the months prior to the VRS attack in July 1995. As the situation deteriorated, the population in the enclave became more insecure and drew closer to the city of Srebrenica. The witness describes the events during the VRS attack, including the movement of the civilian population into Srebrenica, the shelling of DutchBat's Bravo company compound in Srebrenica, and the movement of the population from Srebrenica to the DutchBat compound in Potocari. He describes the scene at Potocari where there were thousands of people who were frightened and insecure gathered around the UN compound. After the takeover of Srebrenica, the witness took part in three meetings at the Hotel Fontana in Bratunac on the 11th and 12th of July, each led on the VRS side by General Mladic. The witness describes at the first meeting the threatening language by General Mladic. The DutchBat commander early in the meeting was being physically enclosed by the VRS persons present and the witness had to push back --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, I will slow down. And the witness had to push back to create some space. DutchBat brought a Bosnian Muslim participant to the second meeting. At the third meeting, there were three Bosnian Muslims present when General Mladic indicated that there would be a so-called screening of male refugees for war crimes. Colonel Boering describes the boarding of buses at Potocari on the 12th of July, the separations of men near the Potocari compound and at the buses there, and the detention of those men in the White House in Potocari. He accompanied the first convoy from Potocari to the Luke-Tisca area where he met VRS Major Sarkic and witnessed men being separated and taken in the direction of the woods by the VRS soldiers. The was asked to escort the women and children through no-man's land to safety in Muslim-held territory. And that concludes the summary. If I may continue on with some questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Shin. If you have any further questions to the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Boering, just some background questions first. Are you still in the military?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, I am. I'm working in Enschede at a school where, for NATO, the UN, and EU where programs for the [indiscernible] are provided both for military personnel and civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And what is your current rank?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: My current rank is that of lieutenant-colonel. Lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'll now move on to some questions relating to the first Hotel Fontana meeting. In your Popovic testimony, you testified that on the 11th of July, DutchBat commander Colonel Karremans, yourself, and DutchBat Sergeant-Major Rave attended a meeting at the Hotel Fontana in Bratunac. This was the first of three meetings at the Hotel Fontana. I'd like to play a few brief segments of a video of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And if I may please have the following segment played. This is from 65 ter 28780, and that's ERN V000-9265. The timing there is from 33 minutes and 33 seconds to 35 minutes and -- I'm sorry. 35 minutes and 53 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before it be played, Mr. Shin, you referred to the testimony in -- in the Popovic case. Could you give us a page reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes. The discussion of this -- of the fact of this meeting on that date would be on page 1941, lines 9 through 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And if I may then please continue with the video at that time segment I had indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, if you could please take a look at the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: "I think General Mladic do not understand well. I'm not the person who requested that specific phase that the Force Commander will have those means available and during the situation, as the situation occurred in the enclave, he will decide. "That request they have considered after a long time. "The only thing I do is, let's say, I put the information through sector in Tuzla to BiH command what's going on in the enclave. Not only military-wise but also for the population, because that is one of my tasks as well humanitarian side of the enclave ... yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Boering, I won't be going through all the identifications in this video of the meeting as that is already set out in your Popovic testimony. But could you just identify from the segment we have just seen who was that who was translating for General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: That was Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Do you know the rank of this Mr. Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: That wasn't clearly visible. He might have been a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You testified in the Popovic case that there were also others at this meeting, including Major Momir Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And for Your Honours, that's referenced at 1943, lines 8 through 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And also a VRS officer named to your recollection either Kosovic or Kosoric, and that would be at page 1948, lines 14 through 25, this latter individual responsible for transporting the refugees. Now, you indicated that these persons were at the meeting though not on the video. How many officers do you recall were at this meeting in total, whether visible on the video of the meeting or not?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I think that, in total, there were about ten from the VRS side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: In your Popovic testimony, you also noted that not all of this meeting was captured on this video. What we saw just now was the beginning of this video, and we see that the -- that the translation was beginning in mid-sentence from the beginning of this video. Approximately how long would you recall that this meeting was underway before this segment of the video begins?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I think that this must have been at least ten minutes. At least ten minutes at the beginning have not been recorded. And also later on in the course of conversations, some parts have not been shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. I would now request to play two more segments, each about one minute long. And I would like to begin at 38 minutes and 41 seconds, going to 39 minutes and 51 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: "No, not again, that's not decided by me. I asked for, that something, what they offer, they make decisions on what I would, on information from the bottom to, let's say even to the United Nations in New York. "Don't do fantasy here, Colonel, and just simply tell me did you give order that two soldiers shoot my soldiers? "I gave the order to defend themselves. That's ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And if we could please then move onto the next one-minute segment, beginning at time 47 minutes and 13 seconds, going to 48 minutes and 15 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: "Assisting the military for ... yeah, I normally do smoke. Normally I do smoke ... but I smoked so much the last days -- "That is concerning the observation post, the OP. That's a personal remark. That I'd like to thank the Bosnian Serb military for treating my soldiers well. "You don't need to thank. That's --"

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Boering, my question to you now that we've seen these segments, in your Popovic testimony, you explained that you and the others felt threatened at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the reference is page 1945, line 17 through page 1946, line 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You also refer specifically in that testimony to General Mladic's comments regarding what might happen if air-strikes were used again. Now, we've just heard that the -- General Mladic explained that these DutchBat soldiers would no longer be hosts and that they know how to bomb too, "they" meaning the VRS, I think we are to understand. That reference to air-strikes by General Mladic, was this the threat that you were referring to in your Popovic testimony?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, that is a clear reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: What was your understanding would happen if there were further air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: If air-strike would have followed, at least the soldiers that have been taken hostage would no longer be treated well and possibly even they could have come under serious threat, and the same could happen to our compound in Potocari or to the refugees. And when one threatens with bombs, then we knew that the Serbs had positions in place surrounding the enclave to do so, so that therefore it was perfectly possible for them to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Boering, earlier in your Popovic testimony, you mention that there had been radio contact from DutchBat soldiers who were imprisoned in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's at 1928 and 1929.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: The radio contact from these soldiers indicated that air support endangered those that who had been taken prisoner so it should stop. You testified in Popovic that you considered that a threat. Just to be clear, who did you understand that threat to be coming from?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: This threat also came from the VRS side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Were you aware of that contact that we just discussed from the DutchBat soldiers imprisoned in Bratunac? Were you aware of that contact before or after this first Hotel Fontana meeting?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I was aware of this prior to the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And how did that knowledge have an effect on your understanding of what you say was General Mladic's threat?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: This was an affirmation of the information I had received previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I would now like to play two more brief segments from this meeting. The first one would be 55 minutes and 37 seconds to 57 minutes and 42 seconds. And the second is 59 minutes, 13 seconds, to 1 hour, 2 minutes, and 10 seconds. So if we could have the first segment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: "... to stop on behalf of the population what had been done, let's say in the last six days. Everybody likes to have a status quo situation and then leave the enclave. And that's on behalf of the civilian population. I asked for, let's say, the safe area around my compound in Potocari through OP-Papa. As being the compound safe area because I'm now there with, let's say, 300 soldiers and more than 10.000 persons. We would like to do as much as possible for the population. "Are you married man, do you have children? "I have two children "For how long you haven't seen them? "Half a year." "Would you like to see them? "Of course."

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And could I have the next segment now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if there's any need for technical assistance, it will be provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic does not have translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we check whether ... Mr. Lukic, fixed? Thank you. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Can we please continue with the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: "What can I say to General Nicolai after we have met here tonight? "You don't have too much good of the conversation with General Nicolai. He cannot help neither you nor the Muslim population. But if you do insist anyway, you tell him ... pass onto him: UNPROFOR troops, no matter of the air-strikes, no matter of your soldiers shooting at my soldiers, are not the goal of mine. Every one of you and your soldiers have only one life, and I do not believe that you would like to leave here. That's why I ask you for absolute co-operation. The goal of my action is also not the Muslim civilian population. I want to help you, even though you do not deserve it. Not as a human nor as an officer. But I will do it for the sake of those children within the UNPROFOR ranks. Because I wouldn't like their mothers to welcome them in coffins. I also want to help to that Muslim civilian population which is also not to be blamed for what happened. That's I would like to ask you the next thing: Are you able and when would you be able to bring here the representatives of civilian population? I would have an arrangement with them. From here you can go out, all of you, or stay, all of you, or die, all of you. And I wouldn't like you to die."

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Boering, my question for you is: Having heard now this -- as we've seen on the video segment, the reference by General Mladic to each DutchBat -- I'm sorry, each DutchBat soldier having only one life, how did you understand that comment during this meeting?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: This was a clear threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now we also heard General Mladic indicating that UNPROFOR was not a goal or objective of the VRS. Did hearing something like that -- did hearing that change your feeling of what you've described as a threatening meeting?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: No, the threat was still in place, if we would only behave in the way that corresponded to Mr. Mladic's ideas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to move to a slightly different topic. This is relating to the DutchBat prisoners. Now, just before the start of this meeting, you discuss in your Popovic testimony seeing the DutchBat soldiers held prisoner at the hotel. You explain in your Popovic testimony that they were "under guard." And that's on page 1942, lines 16 through 20. Mr. Boering, could you please briefly explain what you meant by that phrase, "under guard"?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: A short picture of the situation at Fontana Hotel. I came there regularly so I knew the way there, and when one entered the premises moving towards meeting that we just saw, on the right hand side there was another room, and when passing by the room and looking into it, I saw a group of my colleagues from DutchBat. They were sitting there. They were clearly sitting in a room, unarmed, at a table, accompanied by VRS soldiers, who were armed, and I entered the room shortly, asked them what was happening, what was going on. I had a short conversation with them, and it was clear that they did not have the freedom to leave the room and that they felt under threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Boering. I'd now like to move briefly to the second Fontana meeting. You explained in your Popovic testimony that Colonel Karremans, Sergeant-Major Rave, and yourself had returned to the Hotel Fontana at 11.00 p.m. on the 11th of July with a Bosnian Muslim you had had some earlier contact with.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And general reference, Your Honours, that's at the transcript 1950 and 1951.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I won't be playing any video of this meeting, but I would just like to ask you a couple of questions. Among other persons you'd identified at this meeting, you testified that you had seen Major Momir Nikolic and this VRS officer named Kosoric or Kosovic at this meeting. Do you -- do you recall whether either of these officers were seated at the table during the meeting?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, they were present. Both of them were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And that would be your recollection even if we cannot see them on the video itself; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Without any doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You also had testified in Popovic that --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this is at 1952.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: -- that there were two or three civilians present at the second meeting, and that they had to do with either the police or were otherwise Bratunac authorities. My question for you is: Do you recall whether these individuals were sitting at the table, whether visible on the video or not?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, they were present at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And among these civilian authorities, were some or all of them also present at the third Hotel Fontana meeting?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, all of them also were present at the third meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll now move to the third Hotel Fontana meeting which you testified was to begin at 10.00 a.m. on the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And just the reference on that timing and date would be found on page 1962, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You have -- in your Popovic testimony, have identified persons, several persons who were present at that meeting, so we won't be going through that. I would like, though, to play a brief video segment here. And this is also from 65 ter 28780 from video V000-9266, and the time reference would be 9 minutes, 53 seconds, to 11 minutes 53 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Boering, having watched this video segment, my question for you. We heard a woman ask, How do I get in touch with them? in this video segment. Just so that we're clear, would it be right that that was the woman, a Bosnian Muslim, who had participated in this meeting?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, we can recognise the voice of Camila, someone I know very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And now that was -- that statement was, from the woman, was in response to General Mladic's demand that all the armed men surrender their weapons. Were there any armed Bosnian Muslims in Potocari at this time?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: As for Potocari at this time, I can say the following. Just before the meeting, I walked around there to check the situation, and around the compound in Potocari, there were no signs of any armed Muslim soldiers. One did not see them walking around. I had seen armed soldiers around the place in days previous to the meeting, but not on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now this video is about ten minutes long, and in the Popovic case you had testified that the meeting lasted about half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And that reference is at 1974, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: In this video segment, General Mladic states that when weapons are surrendered, everyone can stay or go. Do you recall if General Mladic said anything at this meeting, whether on the video or not, about what would happen if the weapons were not surrendered?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: If the weapons would not be surrendered, then he would have no doubt that the enclave would come under attack from his troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Is that something he said or is that your interpretation of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: In my view, he actually said this. And he specifically emphasised that we needed to look for representatives of the army, we needed to have contact persons from the army. That was his ultimate wish or his final wish. He could not tolerate any Muslim soldiers to be present in the enclave with arms, and if there would be no clear surrender to them, without any further ado he would attack and bomb the enclave. These have been his words.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Boering, in the -- moving to a slightly different topic. In the Popovic testimony, you also testified about a process of "screening the refugees."

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, that's on transcript pages 1969 through -- oh, 1969 and some of the following pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You had indicated in that testimony that a Serb civilian was introduced by General Mladic as being responsible for "screening" or "inspecting" the refugees for possible war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: That would be at 1969, lines 3 through 11, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You had stated also in the Popovic testimony that you were not at that time able to recall any details regarding this process. Now, do you recall yesterday in reviewing and preparing for your testimony here today, that a portion of your Krstic -- that your testimony in the Krstic case was read to you? Do you recall that? Just yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And -- and did that help refresh your recollection as to which persons would be the subject of this screening?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes. Memory is a relative phenomenon. Sometimes it's worthwhile re-reading one's own statements. And I have to say that the screening of a certain age group has, indeed, been discussed at the meeting, and this specifically concerned men between age 16 and age 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, just for your reference, in the Krstic transcript that would be on pages 1174, line 21, through 1175, line 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that's not in evidence, is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: No. But I -- it was merely used to refresh the witness's recollection. The evidence is what the witness states now. I just mention that for your reference, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin, I am looking at the clock. We're already beyond the one hour for the first session. Could you tell us how much time you would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, my understanding is that we started somewhat late, and I will be able to finish in -- within seven minutes. I believe we will still be within the hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am looking at the Defence, whether it's preferred to have a break now or to continue for another seven minutes. And, Mr. Lukic, if you want to consult with Mr. Mladic, of course, you have an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, he complains that he is tired already, so if we can take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we take a break, and we -- first ask the usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom. We take a break of 20 minute, Mr. Boering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break, and we'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Well, Mr. Mladic, yes, just to check. No one -- everyone was silent, Mr. Mladic, so there was nothing to be translated, but now you hear me, I do understand. We'll wait for the witness to enter the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin, may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Boering, a final question on the topic of the third Fontana meeting. Just before the break, we had discussed a civilian who had been introduced as -- by General Mladic as being a person who would deal with the so-called screening of refugees. My question to you here: Do you recall whether the civilian individual so identified for this process knew one of the three Bosnian Muslims who attended this third Fontana meeting?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall. At the start of the meeting, the representative of the Muslim women, Camila, had a talk with the civilian. And they were talking in their own language so I couldn't grasp what they were saying, but I think they used to be in primary school together, so at the beginning of the meeting they were chatting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Boering. Now the last area that I would like to raise some questions relates to the -- let me put it this way. In your Popovic testimony, you described the arrival of the first convoy from Potocari to a place near Tisca from which the people got off the bus and then proceeded to walk to Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, that would be at 2022 to 2025 in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: At the point where people got off the bus, you testified also that some men were separated by VRS soldiers and led in the direction of the forest but that you were blocked from seeing where they were going ultimately. You also describe on page 2023 speaking to Major Sarkic of the VRS, who you indicate was the person in charge there. My question here is: Do you recall asking Major Sarkic about the separations?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I recall that I had asked him about this. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And what do you recall his response was when you asked him?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: He stated to me that he was getting orders to act so that he simply had to execute orders, that he didn't have a complete picture of what was going on, and he also asked me to -- to mention the number of refugees with whom he would have to deal in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And, just to be clear, then, did he directly respond to your question about the separations?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: In my opinion, he stated that he had to execute the orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Boering.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would now propose to return to the issue of the 92 ter transcript, and if I may ask the remaining questions in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin, of course, attestation, you can ask those questions, which does not mean that we'll are immediately decide on the matter but it is pre-condition for admission. So if we want to consider admission, it's better to have those questions already answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Boering, we had discussed earlier your opportunity to review the testimony from the Popovic case. Now, were you able to identify any clarifications or corrections that you wish to make to that testimony apart from the information you provided today regarding the third Fontana meeting and the information you provided today regarding your discussion with Major Sarkic?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: No. No further information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So if you were asked about these matters today, the matters raised in your Popovic testimony, would you provide the same information in substance as that contained in your Popovic testimony?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I would assume, yes. But, of course, sometimes my recollection is a bit flawed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection today, does your Popovic testimony plus your evidence today capture what you can best recall about the events?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, most certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And having taken the solemn declaration at the beginning of court today, do you affirm that the information in your Popovic testimony is truthful and accurate?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution would tender 65 ter 28791.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was already marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, it has been marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We leave it like that for the time being and the Chamber will further consider admission at the end of the testimony of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Shall I then take up the associated exhibits at the end of the testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it's better to deal with that already now. We'll then include them in the totality of our decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, there will be seven associated exhibits since one has now already been admitted or MFI'd in this case. I'm not aware of any objections, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would list --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- so that Madam Registrar assigns numbers. You say you are not aware of any objections. Mr. Stojanovic, is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So there are no objections against admission. Irrespective of -- but let's -- they're associated. Let's wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you list them then Madam Registrar will assign numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes. The first one is 65 ter 13603.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that would receive number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document receives P1140, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next one, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Next one is 04807.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Receives number P1141, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next one.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Receives number P1142, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Receives number P1143, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Receives number P1144, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Receives number P1145, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Receives number P1146, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, that concludes the questions from the Prosecution in the direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1140 up to and including P1146 are marked for identification. Mr. Stojanovic, are you ready to start your cross-examination? Mr. Boering, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic, and you will find him to your left.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Could you please tell us about your specific duties in the Dutch battalion in 1995.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Within the battalion, which was comprised of about 450 soldiers, there was a headquarters, and the headquarters was comprised of about 15 people. And I was working there and I was attributed to the area of contact, liaison with both VRS and ABiH, civil liaising, and over time also liaising with the military counterparts. So as I said I was the liaison officer. My area had to do with assessing the humanitarian situation, and there was also consultation with both sides. I had to consult with both sides of the military and, if necessary, I had to inform the commander and involve him in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You were affiliated with Sector 5 of your battalion. You were not in the customary chain of command of the battalion. You were directly subordinated to the battalion commander; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: As a HQ member, you are subordinated, indeed, to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you receive your orders from Mr. Franken, who was the deputy battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: That would occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And did you ever report to Mr. Franken on any occasion, whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: No. Let's say that on an almost daily basis there was a consultation with the battalion HQ, and both Karremans and Franken attended those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could one say that you were the best informed officers in the Dutch battalion, that you knew a lot about the situation in the enclave of Srebrenica, given the nature of your tasks and duties?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Let's just say that I was among the better informed, but, of course, there were other people who were equally well-informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was it part of your mandate and the mandate of Sector 5 that you belonged to, to react and disarm any armed members of the BiH army, should such members of BiH army be observed? Were you able to do that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: One of our missions was to disarm the BiH army, so as soon as we spotted that, we had to act. And, of course, in consultation with the Muslim authorities, we tackled this issue. For instance, within the enclave, there was also an arms depot, a Weapons Collection Point, and confiscated weapons, weapons confiscated by DutchBat that is, were subsequently managed by DutchBat. So, yes, we did play a role in that, but direct action was quite difficult a task.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I fully appreciate that. I would like you to tell the Court whether I am right in saying that one part of the demilitarised zone of Srebrenica was an area in which you, members of the battalion, could not access or could not move freely around.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: There was, indeed, an area to which we had limited access. That was the so-called Bandera triangle.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Court, to your best recollection, which part of the demilitarised zone of Srebrenica would that have been?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: It was the western part.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That was an area where the officer of the military unit that was deployed there was Zulfo Tursunovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In 1995, there came a time when the commander of that unit of BiH army took members of the Dutch battalion as hostages. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, I was one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You had a delicate task where you were supposed to try and rescue those men, and then you yourself became a hostage of that same military unit; right?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, how much time did you and the other members of your battalion spend in that situation? How long were you held hostage?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, two or three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you disarmed?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please tell us whether you observed that the members of BiH army who imprisoned you were armed on that occasion in Bandera triangle?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I think I had to surrender my weapons. They took my weapon. And there were also a few locals present there with hunting rifles who were -- who had taken us hostage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the Court's permission, I would to call up 65 ter 19417.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before do you that, Mr. Stojanovic, is your question at line 17 to 19, page 29, answered? It has not been answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood the witness properly, my question was partially answered, and I will pursue the same line of questioning after --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your question was -- your question was,

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: "Will you please tell us whether you observed that the members of the BiH army who imprisoned you were armed on that occasion in Bandera...?" Have you got an answer to that question? I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the interpretation that I'm receiving, the witness said that they were armed, that there were a few locals with hunting rifles. That's on lines 20 and 21 on page 29.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, before we look at the next document, could I remind you that there's no need to repeat questions in cross-examination which are answered in-chief already, such as the Bandera triangle no-go area, whether he was taken hostage or not. That's already clearly already in -- in the transcript. So, therefore, there's no need to repeat anything. Focus your cross-examination on what you want to challenge or what supports your own case. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, just one notice, in relation to document just called, original is not uploaded in e-court or it's uploaded empty. There is only a translation that I'm just publishing now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, any explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to my information, this is a translation. We are interested in page 13. This is a debriefing record that we received from the Prosecutor. I'm interested in page 13, paragraph 203.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, what I see, I see as in -- what is a document which is presented with ET, which means English translation. I do not see any B/C/S translation at this moment. Or is there? Let me just check. And it may be that the original is in another language, not English, not B/C/S. Let me just check. I see the original presented. If I -- if -- if I, in e-court, seek access to the original, it says "no images files were found for this document." So apparently it's not at this moment in e-court. Any objection, Mr. Shin, to working at this very moment on the basis of the English translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, not at this moment. We may be able to assist shortly in obtaining the B/C/S version as well to assist counsel. And it may -- and I do -- like to indicate right now that it may be necessary to bring up the original in Dutch, if the witness would require.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed at this moment, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm showing you this part of the debriefing in which you participated. Could you please explain the part where you say by quoting

utterances.speaker: MR. KARREMANS
utterances.text: "Join in, now are you taken hostage. Go there, see what's going on. In fact, I was not involved in the Bandera triangle at the time. It took place between Franken, Karremans and Zulfo. I personally was not involved in it." I'm asking you what is it that was actually agreed? What is it that actually happened between Franken, Karremans, and Zulfo which had to do with the Bandera triangle incident?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I can't recall the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Among the locals of the demilitarised zone, did you also see people -- people carrying automatic weapons at any occasion?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Towards the end of that period - so that's early July - weapons were carried more often. Prior to that, I hardly ever noted that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During that period of time, you also observed a lot of the locals of the demilitarised zone in new uniforms that they had not worn before that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Are you referring to the period early July?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, could I first seek clarification of paragraph 203. I'll read a portion and then ask a short question to the witness. And, Mr. Boering, you may follow me because you have the document on your screen, I take it. If -- if ... is the document visible for Mr. Boering? Yes. I'm reading from paragraph 203, and I start somewhere in the middle: "As soon as things went wrong, we were just given the assignment: Go have a look and see what the situation is." And then something with question marks. Then: "No, we just drove there, and there was Zulfo." And then: "'Join in, and now you're taken hostage.' "'Go there,' Karremans said, 'see what's going on ...'" Could you tell me the words "join in" and "now you're taken hostage," who is it that spoke those words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember, that must have been Zulfo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I asked you about July. In the month of July, did you observe new equipment and new uniforms sported by locals in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, I did notice that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like us to watch a video-clip, which is 65 ter 28780. It is V000-9265. This is a video-clip featuring the first meeting at Fontana. I would like to ask our dear general to help us. I'm interested in the portions starting at 40 minutes, 30 seconds, and ending at 42 minutes and 37 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: "I've been asked by BiH within the enclave eight times during the last month to give the weapons in the Weapons Collection Point. "How many weapons there were in the collection point? "Do you know? Two -- two battle tanks. "A lot of small arms. "A couple of mortars, and approximately 300 rifles. I rejected that eight times because, in my opinion, and I explained that to the people in the enclave, it won't serve the case for the population. Because we tried to, let's say, to have a status quo situation, and what we have done with the military authorities in the enclave is to collect the weapons which we have seen by patrolling in the beginning, and they have been collected in the Weapons Collection Point. And I'm well aware that there are a lot of arms in the -- in the enclave, and that they have been smuggled from outside the enclave. I have put that many times in the information to the higher military authorities and nationals in Tuzla and Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this clip starts with the following words: Let me hear what you want. This was General Mladic addressing everybody. Who was it who called the first meeting in Fontana hotel? At whose initiative was the meeting organised?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I can't fully reply to that question. I assume that the situation at that point in time was hopeless, which is why I asked to convene a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Am I right in thinking that you were the one who convened the meeting? It was at your initiative? You personally.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: No, it was not my personal initiative. There was always consultation with Karremans. As I said, the situation was hopeless, and I can't remember whether there was a request coming from our side or from Bratunac. I do remember that at one point a meeting time was communicated upon the initiative of Bratunac, and we were also welcome to that meeting. Now, it wasn't unusual for both sides to organise these type of initiatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At one point, you whisper into Colonel Karremans' ear, and we could hear that in the video-clip, There is plenty of small arms. Do you know what happened to those small arms once you abandoned the control of the facility where those small arms were stored, after having been collected there?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: In my opinion, around the 10th of July, we left Srebrenica, together with the refugees, heading for Potocari, and the Weapons Collection Point was then still managed by the Bravo Company. I can't remember any weapons being distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I would like to re-visit an earlier question before we move on. Mr. Boering, you were asked about the initiative for the meeting. Your first answer was -- you explained that the situation was hopeless. And then you said: "... which is why I asked to convene a meeting." Now, in the next -- your answer to the next question, you said: "No, it was not my personal initiative. There was always consultation with Karremans." Now, further down, you said: "I do not know whether the request came from our side or from Bratunac." First, short question: What did you refer to when you say "Bratunac"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bratunac, by that I mean the VRS side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say then, I don't know whether the request came from you or from Bratunac. Then a little bit further down, you said: "A meeting time was communicated upon the initiative of Bratunac, and we were also welcome ..." I mean, who else than UNPROFOR would participate in that meeting? So meeting without you, would that have been a meeting at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A meeting without us would not have been a meeting. There had been a request for a meeting which also included the UN observers in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who else was invited? Oh, you mean the UN observers in -- and UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear to me now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Still, I'm puzzled by you saying, It is hopeless which is why I asked to convene a meeting. And then a couple of lines down, a bit vague who communicated a time for -- one point, a meeting time. I would like to know that very clearly. Was it that you suggested to meet and that they proposed a time, or did they propose to meet? I mean, who said first, Let's meet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Within the battalion consultation, there was discussions with Karremans and I was involved at that, and we agreed that it might have been -- that it would be a good idea to establish contact with the VRS. We had radio contact through walkie-talkie with the Bratunac side. As far as I can remember, it was our side who insisted on it, and it might have been me personally, because I the means of communication, and we did insist on having talks with them. That's at least my recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's a clear answer, it seems. Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, if I may quickly, Your Honours. This may be an opportunity to indicate that 65 ter 19417 has now been fixed, both the English and the -- I'm sorry, both the B/C/S translation and the Dutch original are now available on e-court. If Mr. Stojanovic would intend to take further questions, it may be appropriate to provide the Dutch to the witness. He has indicated his facility with reading English, but he may not have seen a translation of this; only the Dutch version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your information, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have to admit that we had already received a B/C/S version of the text from the Prosecution, although it was not uploaded in the system. We did have it in our possession, physically speaking. I thank you for your assistance, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to conclude the questions concerning the footage of the first meeting where Mr. Karremans says that he was fully aware that there was a lot of weapons in the enclave and that it was also being smuggled out --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: That it had been smuggled into the enclave from outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was that the kind of information you provided to Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans, or did he rely on some other sources from which he learned that weapons were being smuggled into the enclave and that there was plenty of it?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: He obtained this information through the observers and the patrols, patrols organised in the enclave by the DutchBat battalion. He didn't get this from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to ask you this: Did you have personal knowledge of the fact that weapons were being brought into the enclave, thus breaching the agreement on demilitarisation?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, we knew about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will conclude this topic by trying to be practical in my approach. Would you agree with the position that Srebrenica, at the time - that is to say, in the summer of 1995 - was not demilitarised in the sense of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: As of the first week of July, there clearly was a clear armament of ABiH, but then, of course, at the same time, VRS was attacking the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have information that from the enclave itself, there were sabotage operations aimed at the VRS? There was an incident in June 1995 with relation to Visnjica village in that regard.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I am aware of this. I got reports during the briefing, amongst others, with Major Nikolic in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will round off this topic by asking you the following. To the best of your recollection, when were you released from your capture in the Bandera triangle; and, to the best of your recollection, what was the date and month?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I think it was right at the start of my stay. Somewhere around February 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll try to be practical yet again and ask you this: Would you agree with me that during your stay in the demilitarised zone of Srebrenica, were you able to observe that there was an active black market in place, that there were consumer goods available that were being sold and bought at high prices?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: There was, indeed, talk of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you say I was right if I said that throughout your stay in the area and even before your arrival, the corridor between Srebrenica and Zepa functioned unhindered, which ran contrary to the agreement on demilitarisation?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: No. There was smuggling going on between Zepa and Srebrenica, but that occurred along -- alongside our OPs -- or, rather, they bypassed our OPs so our patrols and our observation posts didn't really notice it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, before we take a break, which we'll do in a few minutes, I have one other question for the witness. Are you familiar with the details of the agreement to which Mr. Stojanovic referred a couple of times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not familiar with the details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Stojanovic, if you refer to any agreement, you know that we have had several discussions about several areas with agreements, whether or not in existence, could you always clearly refer to what agreement you're exactly pointing at? Preferably by an exhibit number so that we are able to verify. Now the witness has -- you make a composite question, did this happen, which was in violation of. Now, the witness only answered two times the first part of his question, and he did not express himself on whether it was in violation of. Would you next time if you would be interested to know whether this witness has considered this to be a violation of any agreement, then to be very clear, to ask him specifically about that; and then, second, to point to the agreement itself so that the Chamber is able to follow and to understand the answer. We will take a break. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Lukic, the Chamber was informed that you wanted to address a matter today. I do not know whether you want to do it now or whether you would like to do it at the end of this session. And the Chamber would like to be informed about what the subject is you would like to address, in order to be able to consider whether it's appropriately brought before the Chamber or whether it should be elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can inform you that we are not going to raise that issue today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then that is clear. Thank you for that information. We take a break, and we resume at 20 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we briefly turn into private session for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic. We are now in open session. Would you like to continue in private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, can we go for a minute to closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We move into -- private session would do, I take it, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we have to have a very, very short break, only of two or three minutes, but that's what an urgent matter which needs attention at this moment. Could I ask the witness to be escorted out of the courtroom, but only for two or three minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's not even a need to escort Mr. Mladic out of the courtroom. Just one second, please. One second, please, I asked, but -- let me see. --- Break taken at 12.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience. Mr. Stojanovic, could you give us a -- a more detailed estimate about the time you would need for cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We asked for two and a half hours for this witness. I hope we will be able to stick to that. Maybe we will run approximately ten minutes over, which will be due to the fact that there is double translation, or interpretation, rather. But I hope I will be able to finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, we left it off at the moment when we started talking about the agreement on demilitarisation. You said that you did not have an occasion to read it. I'm asking you now, did you know or were you perhaps briefed about your rights and duties in accordance with that agreement? And I mean did that happen before you were deployed in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes. We were aware of our mandates and our instructions, so we had received training and instruction on these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm moving onto another topic. I would like to talk about the area between Srebrenica and Zepa. Let me ask you: Do you know that the DutchBat wanted to prevent that communication as well as the illegal trade, which is why in April 1995 it started setting up a new observation point in a village called Lozine. And that village is in the southern part of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You also know, don't you, that those attempts met with some resistance by the military and political authorities of Srebrenica, that they opposed those attempts, they didn't want you to establish a new observation post in that area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us look at 65 ter 17846. And while we're waiting for the document to appear, let me tell you that the document was issued by the Command of the 2nd Corps of the BiH Army on the 29th of April, 1995. It instructed the Command of the 28th Division with regard to obstructing the UNPROFOR mandate with regard to that observation point. I'm going to quote from one part of this document where it says -- sir, you may be able to follow -- follow. "With regard to the UNPROFOR attempts in regards the setting up of a new observation post in Lozine, we have to inform you about the following:" Under 1: "The assertion made by UNPROFOR in Srebrenica that, de jure, it has unrestricted freedom of movement and can choose the sites for observation posts in the demilitarised zone of the Srebrenica is accurate (agreement on the demilitarization of Srebrenica and Zepa of 8 May 1993)." Furthermore, in the document, it is suggested in paragraph 3 that: "In light of the above and fully cognizant of the serious negative consequences that the potential establishment of an UNPROFOR observation post would have with respect to the BiH army (jeopardizing the corridor to Zepa), we wish to suggest the following ..." My question is this: Do you remember that UNPROFOR wanted to implement its mandate and prevent communication between Srebrenica and Zepa which is why it was in -- determined to set up that observation post in the village of Lozine?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Within the framework of your mandate, did you manage to establish that observation post or were you prevented from doing so by the locals?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I can remember that it took quite some time to try and establish an observation post there and that, in the end of the day, as far as I can recollect, a site has been chosen but not at the spot that we had envisaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's look at paragraph 4, which is on the following page of the same document. "The 2nd Corps of the BiH army hereby instructs the Command of the 28th Division that the -- the demand to have that observation post set up in the proposed location should be accompanied by a public gathering of the residents of Srebrenica, particularly women and children (a method used by the aggressor with great success on a number of occasions) who are capable of preventing, through organised action, UNPROFOR from setting up an observation post in the village of Lozine sector." Do you remember that there were such actions aimed at obstructing your mandate?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: No, I cannot remember such a thing. I can remember that the, let's say, mayor brought this up. He expressed a dissatisfaction with the idea of establishing observation posts there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, is there any dispute about these matters? I'm looking at you, Mr. Shin, but since Mr. McCloskey is present as well who has an overview of this part of the case, as we understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not aware of any real dispute about OPs or where they're located. I think it's just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And also not about - because that seems to be the issue - obstruction by the armed forces to freely choose where to establish observation posts. No dispute about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any. I -- I know that there -- there will be some evidence of some -- of the Dutch forces being obstructed by both sides. [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but we are now focusing at this moment on, apparently that's what Mr. Stojanovic is doing, is that the ABiH obstructed, more or less, the establishing -- If there's no dispute, Mr. Stojanovic, why spend time on it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if there's no dispute, and if it has been acknowledged that there was a corridor between Srebrenica and Zepa and that that observation post was established in order to prevent communication along that corridor, I don't have any further questions. If the contents of the document have been recognised bearing in mind what the objective of Krivaja 95 was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, the content of the document, of course, is what the document says. Now, whether that's all true and right, et cetera, of course, is a different matter. But I have not heard any questions about that specifically. So try to keep in your mind, Mr. Stojanovic, when proceeding that it seems to be a mainly indisputed subject. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to tender 65 ter 17846.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when I said "indisputed," I don't know whether it's good English. Because something is in dispute, but I take it "undisputed," so I should correct myself. Please proceed. Mr. Shin, anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I believe Mr. Stojanovic had just tendered a document. I was merely going to indicate we had no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, no objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 17846 receives number D272, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. With your leave, I would like to go back to the first meeting at Fontana hotel. I'm asking for the Registrar's assistance with -- at 65 ter 28780, V000-9265. I would like to see the part of the clip starting at 43 minutes, 08 seconds, and ending at 45 minutes, 15 seconds. The clip is a little bit over two minutes long, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: "I had a talk with General Nicolai two hours ago and also with the national authorities about the -- about the request on behalf of the population because I'm not in a position to demand anything. We -- the Command in Sarajevo has said that the enclave has been lost and that I've been ordered by BH Command to take care of all the refugees and are now approximately 10.000 women and children within the compound of Potocari, and the request of BH Command is to, let's say, to negotiate or ask for the withdrawal of the battalion and withdrawal of those refugees and if there are possibilities to assist that withdrawal."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be problem with the audio. I noticed that the volume of the video is very low and by increasing the volume, then it's better. Mr. Lukic, if there's any need to re-play it, just let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we re-play the video, starting with 43:08.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll re-play it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "... we collected all those weapons "What do you want? "I had a talk with General Nicolai two hours ago, and also with the national authorities about the -- about the request on behalf of the population. It's a request because I'm not in a position to demand anything. We ... the Command in Sarajevo has said that the enclave has been lost and that I've been ordered -- ordered by BH Command to -- to take care of all the refugees and are now approximately 10.000 women and children within the compound of Potocari. And the request of the BH Command is to, let's say, to negotiate or ask for the withdrawal of the battalion and withdrawal of those refugees and if there are possibilities to assist that withdrawal."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this clip starts by General Mladic saying, What do you want? You requested a meeting. And then Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans said that he spoke to General Nicolai. And I'm trying to draw your attention to the fact that he said that he had spoken with the national government about the demands of the population. I'm asking you this: Do you know and can you assist us by telling us who was it that Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans spoke to about the demands of the population in Potocari? And he mentioned some national authorities. I'm reminding you that that was said at the first meeting. Can you help us and tell us who that was that Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans spoke to?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the demands of the national authorities on behalf of the population? What was supposed to be done on their behalf?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
